item: Recursive Hilbert-ball coloring of dyadic partitions, driven by a fixed-point-free Lipschitz map
for: Highest item confidence in the pass. Six earlier claimed proofs (Shavgulidze, Akhmedov ×2, Beklaryan, Moore 2012, Wajnryb–Witowicz) never used vector-valued or recursive invariants. A one-line definition turns a 50-year-old problem into about two pages: the Cook–Reckhow profile.
against: Unrefereed (the Lean now compiles and passes Comparator, 2026-10-10). The definition's own reach is narrow: groups that contain F get nonamenability from the theorem, not from the device. The fixed-point-free map itself is transfer (Benyamini–Sternfeld).
next_test: Rerun the device on n-adic cells for F_n without F's transports, then on Stein F_{2,3} and F_τ; compare with and without the colouring in the library.
verdict: The closest match in the corpus to the extension-variable profile. The colour p(T) is a defined object that is absent from the statement and exists only to drive the proof. It dissolves a real obstruction: Følner sets control only averages of bounded functions, while the natural invariant (depth) is unbounded, so the proof needs a bounded invariant that never stabilises. Its ingredient, the Benyamini–Sternfeld map, is transfer (N0). The coupling to F's self-similarity has no precedent found, and six earlier claimed proofs never used a vector-valued recursive invariant, so it looks hard to construct. Two things stand between this and a confirmed jump. (a) The proof is unrefereed; the Lean now compiles and passes Comparator (2026-10-10), so the formal theorem is certified, though the device must still be confirmed to be the one the formal proof uses. (b) The strict definition needs speedups on OTHER theorems, and the definition's own reach looks narrow: groups that contain F inherit nonamenability from the theorem, not from the device, so they test nothing. It may be a one-problem key rather than a jump.
